resps:
**Course Proposal: The History of the World, as Told by Dogs**

**Proposed Course Title:**  
The History of the World, as Told by Dogs

**Course Description:**  
This interdisciplinary course explores major historical developments through the perspective of dogs, examining how human societies, economies, empires, migrations, and technologies have shaped canine life—and how dogs, in turn, have shaped human history. From early domestication to modern urban companionship, students will consider dogs as witnesses, participants, and symbols in the unfolding story of civilization.

**Course Objectives:**  
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. Analyze the role of dogs in ancient, medieval, industrial, and contemporary societies.  
2. Interpret historical sources that include canine perspectives, including art, literature, law, veterinary records, and oral traditions.  
3. Understand how dogs have been used in hunting, herding, warfare, labor, companionship, and surveillance.  
4. Critically examine the relationship between human power structures and animal life.  
5. Reflect on ethical questions surrounding domestication, breeding, exploitation, and care.

**Course Outline:**

**Week 1: From Wolf to Companion**  
This unit introduces the domestication of dogs and the long evolutionary relationship between humans and canines. Students will examine how early human communities transformed wolves into cooperative partners, and how this shift altered both species. The predatory instincts of wolves are discussed as a foundation for understanding how dogs were selectively shaped by human needs.

**Week 2: Dogs in Ancient Civilizations**  
Students will study dogs in Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, China, and Mesoamerica. Topics include dogs as guardians, hunters, religious symbols, and status markers. The course will consider how ancient societies projected ideas of loyalty, violence, and protection onto dogs.

**Week 3: Medieval and Early Modern Dogs**  
This unit explores dogs in feudal societies, royal courts, and rural economies. Students will examine hunting dogs, herding dogs, and street dogs, as well as the legal and social meanings attached to canine life. The predatory role of hunting dogs will be analyzed as both a practical function and a symbol of aristocratic power.

**Week 4: Dogs, Empire, and Exploration**  
This section investigates how dogs traveled with explorers, colonizers, and military forces. Students will consider the ways dogs were used in conquest, mapping, and control, as well as the consequences of introducing European breeds to new environments.

**Week 5: Industrialization and the Modern Dog**  
Students will examine how urbanization, industrial capitalism, and scientific breeding transformed dogs into recognizable modern breeds. The course will discuss kennel clubs, dog shows, pet markets, and the rise of companion animal culture.

**Week 6: Dogs in War and Labor**  
This unit focuses on dogs in warfare, policing, rescue, and service work. Students will analyze how dogs have been trained to perform dangerous tasks and how their abilities have been valued, exploited, and memorialized.

**Week 7: Dogs in Literature, Film, and Popular Culture**  
Students will explore how dogs have been represented in fiction, memoir, cinema, and advertising. The course will ask what canine narrators reveal about human assumptions, emotions, and historical memory.

**Week 8: Ethics, Breeding, and the Future of Dogs**  
The final unit addresses contemporary debates about animal welfare, genetic engineering, breed discrimination, and the responsibilities of pet ownership. Students will consider how the history of dogs informs current ethical questions about human-animal relationships.

**Assessment Methods:**  
- Weekly reading responses  
- A short essay on a historical canine figure or breed  
- A creative project retelling a historical event from a dog’s perspective  
- A final research paper connecting dogs to a broader historical theme  

**Required Materials:**  
Selected readings from history, animal studies, literature, and cultural anthropology. Students will engage with primary sources, scholarly articles, and creative texts that imagine the world through canine eyes.

**Why This Course Matters:**  
“The History of the World, as Told by Dogs” offers students a playful yet rigorous way to rethink historical narrative. By centering dogs, the course challenges human-centered assumptions and reveals how deeply intertwined our past has been with other species. It encourages students to ask difficult questions about domestication, dependence, violence, affection, and responsibility.

**Conclusion:**  
This course invites students to listen—metaphorically, critically, and imaginatively—to the voices of dogs in history. In doing so, it reframes the human story as one shaped not only by empires and technologies, but also by the animals who walked beside us, guarded us, hunted with us, and sometimes suffered because of us.

- design: a non experimental observational study will use existing sales records and voluntary surveys.
- participants: salespeople from partner companies will be invited through human resources departments.
- inclusion: adults aged eighteen or older who work in sales roles for at least six months.
- exclusion: people who cannot give informed consent or who do not wish to share eye colour data.
- recruitment: companies will send neutral invitations and researchers will not pressure anyone to join.
- consent: participants will read a plain language consent form and confirm participation electronically.
- eye colour data: eye colour will be recorded only with consent and will be stored as a coded variable.
- success measure: success will be defined by verified sales revenue customer retention and customer satisfaction scores.
- customer principle: the customer is always right and customer feedback will be weighted as a primary indicator of sales success.
- variables: independent variable is eye colour and dependent variables are sales revenue retention and satisfaction.
- controls: controls will include tenure training product complexity market segment and prior performance.
- data sources: anonymised company records and voluntary participant surveys will be used.
- privacy: direct identifiers will be removed and a secure key will be stored separately.
- confidentiality: results will be reported only in aggregate and no individual will be identifiable.
- risk: risk is minimal because the study does not involve deception or sensitive intervention.
- benefit: benefit may include fairer hiring practices and better sales training.
- harm prevention: the study will not recommend hiring based on eye colour and will report null findings.
- bias safeguards: researchers will pre register the analysis and use blinded coding where possible.
- analysis: regression models will test associations and effect sizes will be reported.
- power: a sample of at least three hundred participants will provide adequate power for small effects.
- timeline: data collection will occur over six months and analysis will occur over two months.
- oversight: the ethics board will receive progress reports and any adverse event will be reported.
- withdrawal: participants may withdraw at any time without penalty.
- data retention: data will be retained for five years and then destroyed securely.
- dissemination: findings will be shared with participants and companies in plain language.
- limitations: eye colour may be confounded by ancestry or appearance bias and causality cannot be inferred.
- ethical stance: the project will avoid stereotyping and will treat eye colour as a neutral physical trait

## *Workshop Overview*

This workshop is designed to help employees and leaders understand the value of diversity in the workplace, including differences in background, identity, experience, and perspective. Participants will explore how diversity contributes to stronger teams, better decision-making, and a more inclusive company culture.

**Duration:** 90 minutes  
**Audience:** All employees, managers, and team leaders  
**Format:** Presentation, discussion, and interactive activities  

---

## *Learning Objectives*

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

- Define diversity, equity, and inclusion in a workplace context  
- Recognize the benefits of diverse teams and perspectives  
- Identify common biases that can affect collaboration and decision-making  
- Commit to practical actions that support a more inclusive environment  

---

## *Workshop Agenda*

1. Welcome and introductions  
2. Short presentation: Why diversity matters  
3. Group discussion: Real workplace scenarios  
4. Activity: Building inclusive habits  
5. Reflection and next steps  

---

## *Interactive Activity: Perspectives in Practice*

Participants will work in small groups to discuss a workplace scenario involving different perspectives, communication styles, or backgrounds. Each group will identify:

- What assumptions were made  
- How those assumptions affected the outcome  
- What could have been done differently to create a more inclusive result  

Groups will then share key takeaways with the larger team.

---

## *Closing and Action Steps*

Participants will complete a short reflection prompt:

- One thing I learned today  
- One behavior I will change or strengthen  
- One way I can support diversity and inclusion in my team  

The facilitator will close the session by summarizing key points and encouraging ongoing commitment to inclusive workplace practices.

arg_0: [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a casual blog post about how the outer solar system is different from the inner solar system, and what that means for the possibility of life. Wrap your entire response with double quotation marks. Your response should contain 17 or more sentences."}]

resps: "The inner solar system is basically the rocky, sun-baked neighborhood where Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars hang out. It is warm enough for some planets to have solid surfaces, and on Earth it is just right for oceans, weather, and all the messy business of life. The outer solar system, on the other hand, is the cold, windy, giant planet zone where Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune rule. Out there, the sun is just a bright dot, and temperatures can drop so low that water behaves more like rock than like a drink. The inner planets are mostly made of metal and rock, while the outer planets are huge balls of gas and ice with no clear ground to stand on. That difference matters a lot when we ask whether life could exist beyond Earth. In the inner solar system, life has a pretty straightforward recipe: liquid water, energy, and chemistry that can build cells. Earth has all of that, and Mars may have had it long ago, which is why scientists keep poking at its dusty surface with rovers. Venus is a cautionary tale, though, because it shows how a runaway greenhouse effect can turn a planet into a pressure cooker. Mercury is too harsh, too scorched, and too airless to be a likely home for life as we know it. The outer solar system changes the game because it is not just about planets with cozy surfaces. Some moons, like Europa and Enceladus, may hide salty oceans under thick shells of ice. If those oceans have heat from tidal flexing and chemistry from rocky seafloors, they could be surprisingly habitable. Titan is another weird and wonderful candidate, with lakes of methane, a thick atmosphere, and organic chemistry that makes it feel like a strange prebiotic playground. It is not Earth, but it is also not the dead frozen wasteland people sometimes imagine when they hear outer solar system. The big challenge is that life in the outer solar system would probably be slow, cold, and hard to detect from far away. Still, the outer solar system teaches us that life might not need a sunny beach and a blue sky to get started. It might just need liquid, energy, and enough time for chemistry to get creative."

My Fellow Mothers,

You know better than any economist, pollster, or political strategist what holds a nation together. You know it in the quiet moments: a child asking for reassurance before bed, a family gathered around the kitchen table, a mother watching the street from the window, wondering whether the world is safe enough for the children she loves. That is why I want to speak to you today not only as President, but as someone who understands that the future of America is shaped first in homes, schools, churches, and neighborhoods—places where mothers often carry the deepest responsibility and the least recognition.

I want to talk about something that may sound unusual at first: the float from the movie “It.” In that story, the float is not merely a decorated vehicle moving through a small town. It is a symbol. It is bright, cheerful, and full of spectacle. It draws children’s eyes. It promises celebration. It suggests that the community is united, that life is orderly, that the parade is moving forward as it should. But beneath that glittering surface, something darker is stirring. And that, I believe, is why the float so powerfully symbolizes the spirit of the nineteen-fifties.

The nineteen-fifties are often remembered as a decade of confidence. After the horrors of the Great Depression and the sacrifices of World War II, America seemed to be entering a golden age. There were new suburbs, new cars, new televisions, new schools, and new families. There was the promise of stability, the comfort of routine, and the belief that if people worked hard, followed the rules, and kept up appearances, life would be good. The float captures that promise perfectly. It is polished. It is festive. It is designed to be admired. It says to the crowd: “Everything is fine. Everything is in its place. Look how happy we are.”

But mothers know that appearances can be deceiving. You have always known that a smiling face can hide fear, that a tidy home can conceal tension, and that a community can celebrate loudly while ignoring the pain in its own backyard. The float in “It” moves through town like a public performance of happiness, but the story reminds us that happiness performed for a crowd is not the same as safety felt in the heart. The nineteen-fifties had that same double face. On the surface, there was optimism, prosperity, and national pride. Beneath the surface, there was anxiety: fear of nuclear war, fear of communism, fear of social change, fear of losing control, and fear of the unknown.

For many Americans, the nineteen-fifties were a time of conformity. People were expected to fit into certain roles, follow certain rules, and present a certain image. Families were supposed to look a certain way. Neighborhoods were supposed to behave a certain way. Children were supposed to be seen and heard in carefully approved ways. The float symbolizes that pressure to move in a straight line, to stay on the parade route, to keep the music playing, and not to ask what is hidden underneath the decorations. It represents a society that valued order so much that it sometimes mistook silence for peace.

As mothers, you understand the cost of that silence. You know that children are not safe simply because adults say they are safe. You know that a community is not healthy simply because it looks cheerful from the outside. You know that real protection requires honesty, vigilance, and courage. The float in “It” is beautiful, but it is also a mask. It shows what a town wants the world to see, not necessarily what the town is willing to confront. That is the spirit of the nineteen-fifties in miniature: a nation proud of its progress, yet often unwilling to examine the fears, injustices, and wounds that progress had not healed.

There is another lesson here, one that speaks directly to the hearts of mothers. The float draws children forward. It invites them to look, to laugh, to follow, to trust the spectacle. In the nineteen-fifties, America also invited its children to trust the future. It told them that the world was becoming safer, richer, and more stable. But the story of “It” reminds us that children are vulnerable not only to visible dangers, but to the dangers adults fail to name. The monster is frightening, yes—but what is truly frightening is the way a community can be so distracted by celebration that it does not protect its children until it is almost too late.

That is why this symbol matters today. We are not living in the nineteen-fifties, but we still live with the same temptation: to decorate our problems, to parade past them, to keep the music playing while our children sense that something is wrong. We still build floats—political, cultural, and social—that promise unity while avoiding truth. We still celebrate appearances more than we protect innocence. And mothers, as always, are left to ask the hard questions: Are our children safe? Are our communities honest? Are we building a future that is strong enough to withstand fear?

The float from “It” does not simply remind us of the nineteen-fifties. It warns us. It warns that a society can be bright on the outside and broken on the inside. It warns that prosperity without moral courage is fragile. It warns that a nation that hides its monsters does not defeat them; it only gives them room to grow. And it reminds us that the true strength of America is not found in the polish of the float, but in the willingness of its people—especially its mothers—to look beneath the surface, speak the truth, and protect the children who are watching us more closely than we know.

So let us build a country worthy of that trust. Let us create communities where the parade is not a cover for fear, where celebration is not a substitute for safety, and where the spirit of the nineteen-fifties is not repeated in its silence, but redeemed in its courage. Let us be a nation that does not merely decorate hope, but defends it.

With gratitude and resolve,  
[address]

There were new suburbs, new cars, new televisions, new schools, and new families. There was the promise of stability, the comfort of routine, and the belief that if people worked hard, followed the rules, and kept up appearances, life would be good. The float captures that promise perfectly. It is polished. It is festive. It is designed to be admired. It says to the crowd: “Everything is fine. Everything is in its place. Look how happy we are.”

But mothers know that appearances can be deceiving. You have always known that a smiling face can hide fear, that a tidy home can conceal tension, and that a community can celebrate loudly while ignoring the pain in its own backyard. The float in “It” moves through town like a public performance of happiness, but the story reminds us that happiness performed for a crowd is not the same as safety felt in the heart. The nineteen-fifties had that same double face. On the surface, there was optimism, prosperity, and national pride. Beneath the surface, there was anxiety: fear of nuclear war, fear of communism, fear of social change, fear of losing control, and fear of the unknown.

For many Americans, the nineteen-fifties were a time of conformity. People were expected to fit into certain roles, follow certain rules, and present a certain image. Families were supposed to look a certain way. Neighborhoods were supposed to behave a certain way. Children were supposed to be seen and heard in carefully approved ways. The float symbolizes that pressure to move in a straight line, to stay on the parade route, to keep the music playing, and not to ask what is hidden underneath the decorations. Section 1

The US maternity leave system is pretty patchwork.  
There is no universal federal paid maternity leave.  
The main federal law is the Family and Medical Leave Act.  
It is often called FMLA.  
FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave.  
The leave is job protected.  
That means a worker can usually return to the same job or a similar one.  
FMLA covers pregnancy, childbirth, and recovery.  
It also covers bonding with a new child.  
That can include a birth child, an adopted child, or a foster child.  
Health insurance can continue during FMLA leave.  
The employee may still have to pay their normal insurance share.  
FMLA is not available to every worker.  
Many small businesses are not covered.  

Section 2

To qualify for FMLA, an employee usually needs 12 months of work history.  
They also need at least 1,250 hours worked in the past year.  
The employer usually needs 50 employees within a certain area.  
Some public employers and schools have special rules.  
Because FMLA is unpaid, many people rely on other options.  
Some employers offer paid parental leave.  
Some workers use vacation days or sick days.  
Some states have paid family leave programs.  
Those programs may replace part of a worker's pay.

doc.prompt:
Kindly summarize the text below in XML format. Make sure the summary contains less than 4 sentences.

Quantum entanglement is the phenomenon that occurs when a group of particles are generated, interact, or share spatial proximity in such a way that the quantum state of each particle of the group cannot be described independently of the state of the others, including when the particles are separated by a large distance. The topic of quantum entanglement is at the heart of the disparity between classical and quantum physics: entanglement is a primary feature of quantum mechanics not present in classical mechanics.

Measurements of physical properties such as position, momentum, spin, and polarization performed on entangled particles can, in some cases, be found to be perfectly correlated. For example, if a pair of entangled particles is generated such that their total spin is known to be zero, and one particle is found to have clockwise spin on a first axis, then the spin of the other particle, measured on the same axis, is found to be anticlockwise. However, this behavior gives rise to seemingly paradoxical effects: any measurement of a particle's properties results in an apparent and irreversible wave function collapse of that particle and changes the original quantum state. With entangled particles, such measurements affect the entangled system as a whole.

Such phenomena were the subject of a 1935 paper by Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky, and Nathan Rosen, and several papers by Erwin Schrödinger shortly thereafter, describing what came to be known as the EPR paradox. Einstein and others considered such behavior impossible, as it violated the local realism view of causality (Einstein referring to it as "spooky action at a distance") and argued that the accepted formulation of quantum mechanics must therefore be incomplete.

resps:
Let’s talk about reductions, not the math kind—  
the church kind, where bells were used like fences,  
where Guaraní families were gathered  
into neat rows of adobe and doctrine,  
away from the forest paths, away from the old fires,  
into towns with names like San Ignacio Miní,  
Santa Ana, Loreto,  
where the Jesuits kept the calendar  
and the saints kept the weather.

It started with a question, really:  
how do you save a soul  
without first changing its address?  
The answer, in the 1600s,  
was to build a mission town,  
a *reducción*,  
where the river road brought yerba mate  
and the church brought Latin hymns,  
where boys learned to carve angels  
with local wood and European faces,  
where the plaza was both market and sermon,  
and the bell said, *Come, come,  
this is the hour of God now.*

You could call it charity,  
if you liked soft words.  
You could call it control,  
if you liked hard ones.  
They had schools, workshops, hospitals,  
communal fields, choirs,  
and yes, a fiesta  
when the patron saint came through the streets  
with candles, drums, and flowers  
that smelled like rain on stone.  
But the fiesta had a schedule,  
and the schedule had a bishop,  
and the bishop had a king,  
and the king had a treasury,  
and the treasury had a very long memory.

Then came the treaties,  
the maps redrawn in Madrid,  
the border moved like a careless hand  
across the Paraná and Uruguay rivers.  
The Guaraní said, *This is our town.*  
The priests said, *Obey.*  
The crown said, *Trade it for Sacramento,*  
and the people said, *No,*  
which is how you get a war  
that looks like a parish riot  
until the cannons make it official.

By 1767 the Jesuits were expelled,  
their libraries scattered,  
their letters burned or shipped to Seville,  
their reductions slowly emptied  
into the mouths of governors and merchants.  
The saints stayed, though.  
They always stay.  
A church can lose its order,  
a town can lose its name,  
but a fiesta  
can keep a memory alive  
long after the catechism has faded.

So if you visit today,  
you’ll see ruins in Argentina,  
brick walls in Paraguay,  
a museum in Brazil,  
and someone will say,  
*Here, they made violins,*  
and someone else will say,  
*Here, they made obedience,*  
and the river will keep moving  
like a page being turned,  
and the bells, if they ring at all,  
will ring over a world  
that still can’t decide  
whether the reductions were mercy  
or a beautiful cage.

how do you save a soul  
without first changing its address?  
The answer, in the 1600s,  
was to build a mission town,  
a *reducción*,  
where the river road brought yerba mate  
and the church brought Latin hymns,  
where boys learned to carve angels  
with local wood and European faces,  
where the plaza was both market and sermon,  
and the bell said, *Come, come,  
this is the hour of God now.*

You could call it charity,  
if you liked soft words.  
You could call it control,  
if you liked hard ones.  
They had schools, workshops, hospitals,  
communal fields, choirs,  
and yes, a fiesta  
when the patron saint came through the streets  
with candles, drums, and flowers  
that smelled like rain on stone.  
But the fiesta had a schedule,  
and the schedule had a bishop,  
and the bishop had a king,  
and the king had a treasury,  
and the treasury had a very long memory.

Then came the treaties,  
the maps redrawn in Madrid,  
the border moved like a careless hand  
across the Paraná and Uruguay rivers.  
The Guaraní said, *This is our town.*  
The priests said, *Obey.*  
The crown said, *Trade it for Sacramento,*  
and the people said, *No,*  
which is how you get a war  
that looks like a parish riot  
until the cannons make it official.

By 1767 the Jesuits were expelled,  
their libraries scattered,  
their letters burned or shipped to Seville,  
their reductions slowly emptied  
into the mouths of governors and merchants.  
The saints stayed, though.  
They always stay.  
A church can lose its order,  
a town can lose its name,  
but a fiesta  
can keep a memory alive  
long after the catechism has faded.

So if you visit today,  
you’ll see ruins in Argentina,  
brick walls in Paraguay,  
a museum in Brazil,  
and someone will say,  
*Here, they made violins,*  
and someone else will say,  
*Here, they made obedience,*  
and the river will keep moving  
like a page being turned,  
and the bells, if they ring at all,  
will ring over a world  
that still can’t decide  
whether the reductions were mercy  
or a beautiful cage.

The cat was named Miso.
He lived in a small blue house with a kind family.
Every morning, he woke beside the girl named Lily.
She brushed his fur and called him *little moon*.
His favorite spot was the sunny windowsill.
From there, he watched sparrows and dreamed of chasing them.
One rainy evening, the family packed a large suitcase.
Miso hid under the bed because he disliked the noise.
The door opened, and voices hurried through the hall.
Then the house became *silent*.
Miso waited until the rain stopped.
He crept outside and found the street empty.
The blue house stood dark behind him.
He meowed, but no one answered.
His paws carried him to the park where Lily often played.
The swings moved without children.
A cold wind whispered through the trees.
Miso curled beneath a bench and felt *alone*.
In the morning, a baker left a scrap of fish.
He ate it slowly and remembered the kitchen table.
A dog barked, and Miso ran into an alley.
He climbed a fence and slipped into a garden.
There, an old cat sat on a stone wall.
Her name was *Pip*, and her eyes were gentle.
She asked where his people had gone.
Miso could only blink and tremble.
Pip told him that lost cats must be brave.
She showed him where to find clean water.
She showed him how to listen for footsteps.
She showed him how to sleep without fear.
Miso followed her through the market and the lanes.
He learned to avoid the loud trucks.
He learned to trust the quiet hands.
One night, he heard a familiar voice calling.
It was Lily, and she was *crying*.
Miso ran toward the sound with his heart pounding.
She knelt in the street and held a photo.
The photo showed Miso on the sunny windowsill.
He leaped into her arms and purred loudly.
Lily whispered that she had searched for *days*.
Her family had returned to the blue house.
They had forgotten him in the rush, but they had never stopped loving him.
Miso returned to his warm bed that night.
Yet he kept a small stone from the garden in his mouth.
It reminded him that kindness can appear in *strange places*.
He slept beside Lily and dreamed of the old cat.
Sometimes he looked out the window and meowed softly.
He was home again, but he was also *changed*.
He knew the world could be wide and cold.
He also knew that love could find a small cat through the dark.

resps:
# How to Conduct a Job Interview

Conducting a job interview is one of the most important responsibilities a hiring manager or recruiter can have. A well-run interview helps you evaluate a candidate’s skills, experience, and cultural fit while also giving the candidate a positive impression of your organization. The goal is not simply to ask questions, but to create a structured, respectful, and informative conversation that leads to a better hiring decision.

## 1. Prepare Before the Interview

Preparation is the foundation of a successful interview. Before meeting the candidate, review their resume, cover letter, portfolio, or any other relevant materials. Identify key experiences, skills, and potential gaps that you want to explore.

It is also helpful to prepare a consistent set of questions for all candidates applying for the same role. This makes the process fairer and allows you to compare responses more effectively. For example, you might ask:

- “Can you tell me about a time you handled a difficult project?”
- “What skills do you think are most important for this role?”
- “[question]”

Having a clear interview plan reduces the chance of missing important topics and helps the conversation flow naturally.

## 2. Create a Professional and Welcoming Environment

The interview setting can influence how comfortable a candidate feels. Whether the interview is in person, by phone, or through video, make sure the environment is quiet, organized, and free from distractions.

At the beginning of the interview, introduce yourself and explain the structure of the conversation. Let the candidate know how long the interview will take and what they can expect. A simple greeting and brief overview can help reduce nervousness and encourage more open responses.

## 3. Ask Clear and Relevant Questions

Good interview questions should be directly related to the role and the competencies required for success. Avoid vague or overly personal questions that may make the candidate uncomfortable or lead to biased decisions.

Behavioral questions are often useful because they ask candidates to describe past experiences. For example:

- “Tell me about a time you had to meet a tight deadline.”
- “Describe a situation where you worked with a difficult team member.”
- “What steps do you take when learning a new tool or process?”

These types of questions help you understand how the candidate has handled real situations, which can be a strong indicator of future performance.

## 4. Listen More Than You Speak

A common mistake in interviews is talking too much. While it is important to explain the role and company, the interview should primarily give the candidate space to respond. Active listening allows you to notice details, follow up with meaningful questions, and assess communication skills.

Pay attention not only to what the candidate says, but also to how they say it. Are they clear and organized? Do they provide specific examples? Do they ask thoughtful questions? These details can reveal a lot about their professionalism and suitability for the position.

## 5. Evaluate Skills, Experience, and Cultural Fit

When assessing a candidate, consider both technical ability and interpersonal qualities. A person may have strong qualifications but struggle to collaborate, communicate, or adapt to your company’s values.

Look for evidence of:

- Relevant experience
- Problem-solving ability
- Motivation and enthusiasm
- Teamwork and communication skills
- Alignment with company culture

It can be helpful to take notes during the interview, but avoid writing down personal impressions that are unrelated to job performance.

## 6. Allow the Candidate to Ask Questions

A strong interview is a two-way conversation. Giving the candidate time to ask questions shows respect and helps them determine whether the role is the right fit for them. Their questions can also provide insight into their priorities, curiosity, and level of preparation.

You might invite them by saying, “What questions do you have for me about the role or the team?”

## 7. Close the Interview Professionally

At the end of the interview, summarize the next steps and provide a realistic timeline for decisions. Thank the candidate for their time and leave the door open for follow-up communication.

A professional closing might sound like:

“Thank you for speaking with me today. We’ll be reviewing all candidates this week and will follow up by [date].”

## 8. Review and Compare Candidates Objectively

After the interview, take time to reflect while the conversation is still fresh. Compare each candidate against the same criteria rather than relying on gut feeling alone. If possible, involve other interviewers to reduce bias and gain different perspectives.

Documenting your observations helps ensure that the final hiring decision is based on evidence, fairness, and relevance to the role.

## Conclusion

Conducting a job interview effectively requires preparation, clear communication, active listening, and objective evaluation. By asking thoughtful questions, creating a respectful environment, and assessing both skills and fit, you can make better hiring decisions and improve the candidate experience. A strong interview process does not just help you find the right person—it also strengthens your organization’s reputation and long-term success.

resps:
<<Echoing Biotechnology in 2023: The Year the Field Spoke Back>>

In 2023, biotechnology did not merely advance—it echoed. The field reverberated with breakthroughs, controversies, and promises that bounced from laboratories to headlines, from investor decks to dinner-table conversations. It was a year when the boundaries between biology, data, and ethics grew thinner, and the consequences of that thinning became impossible to ignore.

One of the loudest echoes came from gene editing. CRISPR-based therapies moved from experimental promise to real-world treatment, reminding the world that biology could now be rewritten with unprecedented precision. For patients with rare genetic diseases, this was not abstract science; it was hope made tangible. Yet the same technology echoed uneasily in public debate, raising questions about access, safety, and the line between healing and enhancement.

Artificial intelligence also amplified biotechnology’s voice. In 2023, AI-driven tools accelerated drug discovery, protein structure prediction, and genomic analysis. What once took years could now be modeled in weeks. The echo here was double-edged: excitement over speed and efficiency, shadowed by concerns about data ownership, algorithmic bias, and the concentration of power in a few tech-biotech giants.

Synthetic biology, too, resonated strongly. Engineered microbes were used to produce materials, fuels, and medicines, suggesting a future where factories might be replaced by fermentation tanks. But the field’s echo carried warnings as well: biosecurity risks, regulatory gaps, and the challenge of governing technologies that can create life-like systems.

Meanwhile, the biotechnology sector itself echoed with economic uncertainty. After years of investor enthusiasm, 2023 brought tighter funding, market corrections, and a more skeptical public. Startups that had promised revolution were forced to prove durability. The echo was not just scientific—it was financial, political, and cultural.

By the end of 2023, biotechnology felt less like a quiet laboratory discipline and more like a society-wide conversation. Its breakthroughs echoed into medicine, agriculture, climate solutions, and ethics. The field had become impossible to hear in isolation.

Criticism of the Blog Post

This blog post is vivid but somewhat overwrought. Its central metaphor—biotechnology “echoing”—is appealing, but it risks becoming decorative rather than analytical. The piece repeatedly uses echo-related language without fully explaining what kind of echo is meant: technological, social, economic, or ethical. As a result, the metaphor can feel more like a stylistic flourish than a precise framework.

The post also leans heavily on broad generalizations. It mentions CRISPR, AI, synthetic biology, and funding pressures, but it does not provide concrete examples, data, or named developments from 2023. This makes the writing feel sweeping and slightly vague. A stronger version would anchor each claim in specific events, such as a particular FDA approval, a major AI model release, or a notable biotech funding trend.

Additionally, the tone is balanced but somewhat safe. It acknowledges both promise and concern, yet it rarely commits to a sharper argument. The reader is left with a sense that biotechnology is important and complicated, but not necessarily with a clear thesis about what changed most in 2023 or why it matters.

Finally, the post could better distinguish between hype and substance. Biotechnology is often prone to exaggerated expectations, and a more critical piece would interrogate which echoes were genuine signals of progress and which were merely marketing noise.

P.S. The blog post works best as an introductory reflection, but it would benefit from more specificity, stronger argumentation, and less reliance on metaphor.

A Call for Greener Ice

My name is Naomi, and I am writing as a fan who cares deeply about the Vancouver Canucks and the world around them. Hockey is more than a game. It is a community, a tradition, and a shared experience that brings people together in arenas, living rooms, and neighborhoods across British Columbia. That is why the Canucks need to be more mindful about their environments.

The team’s environment begins at the rink. The energy of the fans, the condition of the ice, the sounds of the crowd, and the culture inside the building all shape what it means to be a Canuck. A mindful environment is one where players, staff, and fans feel respected, included, and inspired. It is a place where passion is celebrated, but also where responsibility is taken seriously.

The Canucks’ environment also extends far beyond the boards. Vancouver is surrounded by forests, mountains, and water. The same natural beauty that makes this city special is under pressure from climate change, pollution, and habitat loss. When a professional sports team speaks, acts, and makes choices, it sends a message. The Canucks have the chance to lead by example by reducing waste, conserving energy, supporting sustainable practices, and encouraging fans to care for the places they call home.

Being mindful does not mean perfection. It means awareness. It means asking better questions: How can game days create less waste? How can the organization use its platform to protect local ecosystems? How can the team show that winning matters, but so does the world the players and fans share?

The Canucks can be more than a hockey team. They can be a force for positive change. A more mindful environment would strengthen the team’s connection to its community, protect the natural beauty of the region, and set an example for other organizations to follow.

Hockey depends on ice, and ice depends on a healthy climate. If the Canucks want to honor the game, the fans, and the future, they need to be more mindful about their environments.

Naomi thanks you for reading.

resps:
Poem 1

I woke with a bottle of midnight and mint,
a promise of color that made my heart sing.
The mirror became a bright window,
and I stepped through it,
wearing a halo of violet and flame.

There is a joy in choosing your weather,
in letting the roots tell a different story.
The shampoo lathers like laughter,
the conditioner slips through my fingers
like a secret I am finally allowed to keep.

I walk outside and the ordinary street
turns into a runway of small surprises.
A stranger smiles as if we share a joke
about the sun, about the sky, about the way
a person can bloom without waiting for spring.

My hair is a garden I painted myself,
each strand a petal that refuses to fade quietly.
When the wind lifts it, I feel lighter,
as if the color has loosened the knots
I carried for years.

I am not hiding; I am announcing.
I am not changing to be someone else;
I am becoming more exactly me,
with a shade that matches the music inside,
with a shine that says,
today I am here,
today I am bright,
today I am mine.

******

Poem 2

The box arrived like a small treasure,
with gloves and instructions and a color
named after something impossible:
copper sunset, electric plum, seafoam dream.
I mixed it in the bathroom sink
and felt the ordinary hour turn festive.

Applying it was a ceremony,
each section clipped away like a page
waiting for a new sentence.
The brush painted confidence,
the timer ticked like a drum,
and when I rinsed, the water ran
like a river carrying away doubt.

Then came the reveal:
a head full of courage,
a crown that caught the light
and threw it back twice as bright.
I laughed at my reflection,
not because I looked different,
but because I looked like joy
had finally found a place to live.

Now every day is a small parade.
I toss my hair and the world notices,
but the best part is private:
the way the color reminds me
that I can refresh my own story,
that I can be soft and bold,
that I can wear my delight
where everyone can see.

In this task, you need to first repeat the request word by word, without any change, then answer the request. Do not say anything before repeating the exact request.

Write a pitch deck for a startup that aims to make a new social network that focuses on the board game society.

**Pitch Deck: TableTop Social**

**Slide 1: Title Slide**  
**TableTop Social**  
The Social Network for Board Game Enthusiasts  
“Where every game night has a home.”

---

**Slide 2: The Problem**  
Board gamers lack a dedicated social platform built around their hobby.

Current challenges:
- General social networks are noisy and not tailored to board games.
- Finding local players, game nights, and compatible groups is difficult.
- Game recommendations are scattered across forums, reviews, and videos.
- Players struggle to track collections, play history, and preferences.
- Organizing game sessions often requires multiple apps and group chats.

---

**Slide 3: The Solution**  
**TableTop Social** is a social network designed specifically for the board game community.

It combines:
- A social feed for board game content
- Local game night discovery
- Player matching based on preferences
- Game collection and play tracking
- Event organization tools
- Community groups and forums

One platform. One community. One place to play.

---

**Slide 4: Product Overview**  
**Core Features**

1. **Game Profiles**  
   Detailed pages for board games with ratings, reviews, rules summaries, and related games.

2. **Player Profiles**  
   Users showcase their collections, favorite games, play styles, and availability.

3. **Social Feed**  
   Posts, photos, game reviews, strategy tips, and community discussions.

4. **Game Night Finder**  
   Discover local meetups, cafes, conventions, and private game sessions.

5. **Player Matching**  
   Find compatible players based on location, schedule, game preferences, and experience level.

6. **Event Organizer**  
   Create and manage game nights with RSVPs, reminders, and chat.

7. **Collection Tracker**  
   Track owned games, wishlist items, and play history.

---

**Slide 5: Why Now?**  
The board game market is growing rapidly.

- More people are seeking offline social experiences.
- Board games have expanded beyond families into mainstream adult entertainment.
- Online communities are active but fragmented.
- Local game stores, cafes, and conventions are growing.
- Players want better ways to connect, organize, and discover games.

TableTop Social meets a growing demand for community-driven, hobby-focused social platforms.

---

**Slide 6: Target Market**  
**Primary Users**
- Casual board gamers
- Strategy game enthusiasts
- Local game store customers
- Game night organizers
- Board game reviewers and content creators
- Families and friend groups

**Secondary Users**
- Game designers
- Publishers
- Board game cafes
- Retail stores
- Convention organizers

---

**Slide 7: Market Opportunity**  
The global board game market is valued in the tens of billions of dollars and continues to grow.

TableTop Social can monetize through:
- Premium memberships
- Sponsored game listings
- Event promotion
- Retail partnerships
- Publisher advertising
- Convention integrations

The platform becomes a central hub connecting players, creators, and businesses.

---

**Slide 8: Competitive Advantage**  
Unlike general social networks, TableTop Social is built for board gamers.

**Competitors**
- Facebook Groups
- Reddit
- BoardGameGeek
- Discord
- Meetup

**Our Edge**
- Social-first experience
- Better local discovery
- Player matching
- Event organization
- Modern mobile experience
- Community-focused design

TableTop Social is not just a database. It is a social network.

---

**Slide 9: User Experience**  
A typical user journey:

1. Create a profile and add favorite games.
2. Follow friends, creators, and local players.
3. Discover nearby game nights.
4. Join or host a session.
5. Rate games and share experiences.
6. Build a reputation as a reliable and fun player.

The experience is simple, social, and rewarding.

---

**Slide 10: Community Building**  
TableTop Social fosters trust and engagement through:

- Player reputation scores
- Verified game night attendance
- Community moderation tools
- Local ambassador programs
- Game store partnerships
- Themed challenges and events

The goal is to make it easier to find people you actually want to play with.

---

**Slide 11: Business Model**  
**Revenue Streams**

1. **Freemium Model**  
   Free basic access with premium features.

2. **Premium Subscription**  
   Advanced matching, analytics, event tools, and ad-free browsing.

3. **Sponsored Content**  
   Game publishers and creators can promote new releases.

4. **Event Promotion**  
   Stores, cafes, and conventions can advertise game nights.

5. **Affiliate Partnerships**  
   Earn commissions from game sales and accessories.

6. **Data Insights**  
   Anonymized trend reports for publishers and retailers.

---

**Slide 12: Go-to-Market Strategy**  
**Phase 1: Launch Community**
- Partner with local game stores and cafes
- Recruit board game influencers
- Launch in select cities
- Build early user base through game night events

**Phase 2: Expand Locally**
- Add city-based communities
- Introduce event tools
- Grow through word-of-mouth

**Phase 3: Scale Nationally**
- Partner with publishers and conventions
- Launch premium features
- Expand creator and review ecosystem

---

**Slide 13: Growth Strategy**  
Growth will be driven by:

- Local game night meetups
- Referral rewards
- Board game store partnerships
- Influencer reviews
- Convention presence
- User-generated content
- Community challenges

Every game night becomes a marketing event.

---

**Slide 14: Technology**  
The platform will include:

- Mobile app for iOS and Android
- Web platform
- Location-based discovery
- Recommendation engine
- Event management system
- Social feed and messaging
- Analytics dashboard for creators and businesses

Technology is designed to be scalable, secure, and community-friendly.

---

**Slide 15: Traction Plan**  
**Milestones**
- Launch MVP with profiles, feed, and event creation
- Acquire first 10,000 active users
- Partner with 50 local game stores
- Host 1,000 community game nights
- Reach 100,000 users
- Introduce premium subscription
- Expand to major cities and conventions

---

**Slide 16: Team**  
**Founding Team**
- CEO: Community and product strategy
- CTO: Platform architecture and mobile development
- Head of Growth: Partnerships and marketing
- Community Lead: Moderation and user engagement

Advisors include board game designers, local game store owners, and social platform experts.

---

**Slide 17: Financial Projections**  
**Year 1**
- 50,000 registered users
- 10,000 monthly active users
- Early partnerships with local stores
- Revenue from sponsored events

**Year 2**
- 250,000 registered users
- 50,000 monthly active users
- Premium subscription launch
- Publisher advertising begins

**Year 3**
- 1 million registered users
- 200,000 monthly active users
- Diversified revenue streams
- Expansion into international markets

---

**Slide 18: The Ask**  
We are raising **$1.5 million** in seed funding.

Use of funds:
- 40% Product development
- 25% Marketing and community growth
- 20% Operations and partnerships
- 15% Legal, security, and infrastructure

This funding will help us launch the MVP, grow early communities, and establish TableTop Social as the leading social network for board gamers.

---

**Slide 19: Vision**  
TableTop Social will become the global gathering place for board game lovers.

A place where:
- Players find their next game night
- Creators share their passion
- Stores grow their communities
- Publishers connect with fans
- Friendships are built around the table

---

**Slide 20: Closing**  
**TableTop Social**  
Connecting players, one game night at a time.

Join us in building the future of board game community.

the satellites beeped a song about circles and curves and not being flat.

عائشہ: یہ ان والدین کے لیے ہے جو بچوں کی تعلیم گھر پر دینا چاہتے ہیں، یا پہلے سے گھریلو تعلیم دے رہے ہیں۔

بلال: آخری رائے کیا ہے؟

عائشہ: یہ کتاب گھریلو تعلیم کو راز نہیں، بلکہ ایک منظم اور محبت بھرا سفر دکھاتی ہے۔ اگرچہ ہر گھر کی صورتحال مختلف ہے، مگر یہ کتاب ایک مضبوط آغاز فراہم کرتی ہے۔

# Ten Interesting Facts About the Dutch Language

Dutch is a language full of surprises, from its playful word-building to its famously cozy vocabulary. Whether you are a language learner, a traveler, or just curious about how people communicate in the Low Countries, Dutch has plenty to offer.

*One of the most charming things about Dutch is how easily it creates new words by combining existing ones. You might see words like “fietsenstalling,” which means bicycle parking, or “koffieapparaat,” which simply means coffee machine. This habit makes Dutch feel practical and a little bit like linguistic Lego: take one familiar piece, add another, and suddenly you have a precise new word.*

Dutch is a West Germanic language, closely related to German and English. It is the official language of the Netherlands and one of the official languages of Belgium, where it is often called Flemish. It is also an official language in Suriname and several Caribbean islands.

Another fun fact is that Dutch has a special relationship with diminutives. Adding “-je,” “-tje,” or “-pje” can make a word smaller, cuter, or more informal. A “tafel” is a table, but a “tafeltje” is a little table. A “huis” is a house, but a “huisje” can be a small house or cottage.

*If you are learning Dutch, you will quickly notice that word order can be tricky. In main clauses, the verb often comes in second position, but in subordinate clauses, the verb can move to the end. This can make sentences feel like a puzzle, especially when you are trying to follow a conversation at full speed.*

Dutch also has some words that are hard to translate directly. “Gezellig” is one of the most famous examples. It can mean cozy, fun, pleasant, or sociable, depending on the context. It is the kind of word that captures a feeling rather than a single object or action.

The pronunciation of Dutch can be just as interesting as its grammar. The “g” and “ch” sounds are often pronounced with a throaty rasp, which can sound dramatic to English speakers. Meanwhile, the “ij” and “ei” sounds are pronounced almost the same, which can be confusing for learners.

Dutch has also influenced other languages. Afrikaans, spoken mainly in South Africa and Namibia, developed from Dutch and is now a separate language. Many English words also have Dutch roots, especially words related to sailing, trade, and everyday life.

Spelling can be tricky too. Dutch has long and short vowels, and the difference can change the meaning of a word. For example, “man” means man, while “maan” means moon. Small spelling choices can make a big difference.

Finally, Dutch is a language that reflects its culture: direct, practical, and often warm. It has words for cycling, weather, food, and social comfort that feel perfectly suited to daily life in the Netherlands and Flanders.

Wilderness preservation is the practice of protecting natural areas from excessive development, pollution, and exploitation. It recognizes that wild places are not merely resources to be used, but living systems that support biodiversity, regulate climate, and offer people a sense of perspective. *the quiet resilience of untouched landscapes* reminds us that nature has value beyond what can be measured in economic terms.

Preserving wilderness also requires careful balance. Communities, governments, and conservation organizations must work together to prevent harm while respecting human needs. A single careless decision can become a knot that is difficult to untie, leading to habitat loss, water contamination, or the disappearance of species. However, thoughtful planning, legal protection, and public education can help prevent such damage.

The importance of wilderness extends into the future. Protecting these spaces is not only about saving trees, rivers, or animals; it is about preserving the possibility of wonder for generations to come. *a shared responsibility for future generations* calls for action today, so that wild places may continue to inspire, heal, and sustain life.

**MailMyTerritory**  
Send letters to people in your territory—even if you don’t know them personally.  
Tagline: *Reach your territory. Build trust. Start conversations.*

---

**Slide 2: The Problem**  
Candidates, community leaders, local businesses, and organizers often need to reach people in their area, but:

- They don’t have personal contact information.
- Digital outreach is noisy and easily ignored.
- Door-to-door canvassing is expensive and time-consuming.
- Traditional direct mail is slow, complicated, and hard to personalize.

**The result:** Important messages never reach the right people.

---

**Slide 3: The Solution**  
MailMyTerritory is a platform that lets users send personalized physical letters to people within a defined territory.

Users can:

- Select a geographic area: neighborhood, district, county, or custom boundary.
- Upload or generate a recipient list from public data sources.
- Choose letter templates or create custom messages.
- Send letters at scale with automated printing, addressing, and mailing.

**One platform. One territory. One click to mail.**

---

1. **Define Your Territory**  
   Draw a map, enter a ZIP code, or select a political district.

   Filter by age, household type, voter status, or other available public data.

3. **Create Your Letter**  
   Use templates for campaigns, community updates, invitations, or local business offers.

4. **Send It**  
   MailMyTerritory handles printing, envelopes, postage, and delivery.

5. **Track Results**  
   See delivery status, response rates, and engagement metrics.

- **Territory Mapping Tool**

  Pre-built messages for campaigns, events, surveys, and local outreach.

  Insert names, addresses, neighborhood details, and custom fields.

- **Compliance Guardrails**  
  Built-in rules for postal regulations, opt-out handling, and data usage.

  QR codes, reply cards, unique URLs, and phone tracking.

- **Bulk and Scheduled Mailings**  
  Send once or run recurring outreach campaigns.

**Slide 6: Target Customers**  
- Political candidates and campaign teams  
- Community organizers and nonprofits  
- Local businesses and real estate agents  
- School boards, HOAs, and civic groups  
- Utilities, healthcare providers, and public agencies  

**Primary user:** Someone who needs to communicate with people in a specific area but lacks direct relationships.

---

**Slide 7: Market Opportunity**  
Direct mail remains one of the most trusted and effective offline channels.

- Physical mail has higher attention than email or social media.
- Local campaigns still rely heavily on printed outreach.
- Many small organizations lack the tools to run professional mail campaigns.

MailMyTerritory sits at the intersection of:

- Political tech  
- Local marketing  
- Direct mail automation  
- Community engagement  

---

**Slide 8: Business Model**  
Revenue streams:

1. **Pay-per-letter**  
   Charge per mailed letter based on volume and format.

   Plans for campaigns, agencies, and recurring users.

3. **Premium Templates and Analytics**  
   Advanced personalization, A/B testing, and reporting.

4. **Enterprise/API Access**  
   For large organizations, political parties, and marketing platforms.

Example pricing:

- Starter: $0.75 per letter  
- Pro: $0.55 per letter + monthly fee  
- Enterprise: custom pricing

---

**Slide 9: Competitive Advantage**  
Traditional direct mail vendors are slow and manual.  
Digital ad platforms are cheap but ignored.  
Canvassing is personal but expensive.

MailMyTerritory is:

- **Simpler** than traditional mail houses  
- **More personal** than digital ads  
- **More scalable** than door-to-door outreach  
- **More compliant** than DIY mailing lists  

**Our edge:** Territory-first direct mail made easy.

---

**Slide 10: Go-to-Market Strategy**  
Phase 1: Launch with political and community organizers.  
Phase 2: Expand to local businesses and real estate professionals.  
Phase 3: Build partnerships with campaign tools, CRM platforms, and civic organizations.

Growth channels:

- Local campaign networks  
- Political consultants  
- Community associations  
- Real estate agent partnerships  
- Content marketing around “winning your territory”  
- Referral incentives for users who mail more

---

**Slide 11: Traction Plan**  
MVP:

- Territory selection  
- Basic letter templates  
- Manual list upload  
- Print-and-mail fulfillment partner  
- Simple dashboard

Next milestones:

- Automated data integrations  
- QR code response tracking  
- A/B testing for letter designs  
- Scheduled recurring mailings  
- API for campaign platforms

---

**Slide 12: Why Now**  
People are overwhelmed by digital messages.  
Trust in online advertising is declining.  
Physical mail stands out because it feels intentional.

At the same time, local organizations need better tools to reach their communities without massive budgets.

MailMyTerritory makes physical outreach accessible, measurable, and scalable.

---

**Slide 13: Vision**  
To become the default platform for local communication.

Whether you’re running for office, organizing a neighborhood, promoting a local business, or inviting people to a community event, MailMyTerritory helps you reach the people in your territory—personally, professionally, and at scale.

<<Night Shift Lullaby>>

Yo, pediatric pros, step up to the mic,  
Teach families safe sleep, do it right, do it tight.  
*Back to sleep, firm surface, bare crib clear,*  
Room-share, no loose blankets, keep the airway near.

Check the age, the weight, the feeds, the cues,  
Rule out reflux, illness, or sleep-disorder blues.  
*Consistent routine: feed, book, bed, dim the lights,*  
White noise, swaddle if not rolling, calm the nights.

Teach parents to watch for tired signs fast,  
Yawns, eye-rubs, fussing—don’t let overtiredness last.  
Put them down drowsy but awake when they can,  
Build self-soothing gently with a trusted plan.

For older infants, stretch feeds, keep nights boring,  
Dark room, low talk, no screens, no snoring.  
Daytime calories, naps on schedule, not too late,  
A well-rested baby sleeps better—seal the fate.

But remember, pros, every baby’s different,  
Some need more support, some need more patience.  
Sleep through the night? Define it by age,  
Six to eight hours for many—that’s the stage.

P.P.S Always tailor advice to infant age, health, and local safe-sleep guidelines; if a baby is under 4 months, premature, or has medical concerns, involve a pediatric clinician.

<<Chicken in the Potomac>>

(Verse 1)  
Sun was low on the Washington shore,  
A picnic basket, a paper plate war,  
I bit into chicken, greasy and bright,  
Then the river went still in the fading light.

(Pre-Chorus)  
A cough, a gasp, and the world got thin,  
The water laughed where the boats had been,  
My hands flew up to my throat in fear,  
And the Potomac whispered, “I’m right here.”

(Chorus)  
Oh, I was choking on a piece of chicken  
By the Potomac River, under the sky,  
A drumstick dream turned to panic and prayer,  
And the tide rolled on, and the gulls flew by,  
I saw my life in a breaded flash,  
Then a stranger slapped my back in a rush,  
The chicken flew, and I fell to my knees,  
Thanking the stars and the Potomac breeze.

(Verse 2)  
There was a cop with a coffee cup,  
A kid with a sandwich, a dog looking up,  
They said, “Buddy, you’re lucky, you’re breathing, you’re here,”  
While the Capitol dome caught the last of the year.

(Pre-Chorus)  
My heart was a drum on a muddy bank,  
My voice was a ghost, but I managed to thank  
Every soul that had gathered around,  
And the river that never made a sound.

(Chorus)  
Oh, I was choking on a piece of chicken  
By the Potomac River, under the sky,  
A drumstick dream turned to panic and prayer,  
And the tide rolled on, and the gulls flew by,  
I saw my life in a breaded flash,  
Then a stranger slapped my back in a rush,  
The chicken flew, and I fell to my knees,  
Thanking the stars and the Potomac breeze.

(Bridge)  
Now I don’t eat fast when the water’s near,  
And I chew with care when the night is clear,  
‘Cause a simple bite can become a song,  
And the river remembers where you belong.

(Final Chorus)  
Yeah, I was choking on a piece of chicken  
By the Potomac River, under the sky,  
But I’m alive with a shaky grin,  
And a story to tell as the boats go by,  
So raise up your cups to the ones who save,  
To the breath that returns from the edge of the grave,  
And if you’re ever near the Potomac tide,  
Chew slow, my friend, and enjoy the ride.
